sections.html:
Harrisburg is a state capital where most homes are rented, prices are modest and many sellers are landlords or heirs. The 2025 estimate is 50,522 people, and the 2020 to 2024 survey counts 22,137 households. Only 36.6 percent of occupied homes are lived in by their owners. A typical owned home is worth $124,200, rent runs $1,062 and the median household income is $48,099.

Investors who price a house by its rent roll are common buyers, and lenders can be wary of a property that needs work. A vacant or tenant-occupied Harrisburg house may suit a buyer who takes it as it stands. The city's older rowhouses and brick twins often need updates, which is part of why cash buyers are active here.

sections.h2: Is your address inside the city?
sections.html:
Harrisburg sits on the east bank of the Susquehanna River and is the seat of Dauphin County and the capital of Pennsylvania. Be careful with addresses. Several nearby townships, including Lower Paxton and Middle Paxton, use Harrisburg as their mailing name even though they sit outside city limits and follow their own codes. Check whether your parcel is inside the city before you read any rule below. Your tax bill or the county parcel record shows which municipality bills you.

Inside the city, six municipal historic districts, several national historic districts and architectural conservation overlays guide new work in older blocks, so ask before you change an exterior.

The city's Bureau of Codes handles building permits, trade licenses, rental registration and property complaints, and you can reach it at 717-255-6553. Harrisburg follows the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, with the 2021 international code editions.

  • Permits are required for roofing, fences, sheds, decks, replacement windows and doors, any structural work, new furnaces and any work above $1,000.
  • Residential permit applications must be decided within 15 business days, or 5 days if a design professional stamps the plans. Historic Review Board review adds time.
  • A building permit expires after 6 months if work is not continuous.
  • Electricians and plumbers must hold a city license, and every contractor needs a city business privilege license.
  • The Bureau Health Officer enforces lead-based paint hazard rules for residential structures.

If you did work in the past without a permit, call the Bureau before you list. That way you know what is open on the property before a buyer asks.

Older Harrisburg houses often carry deferred work: roofs, windows, furnaces and structural repairs are the items that trigger permits. If a past owner did that work without a permit, the buyer's inspector or lender can raise it. Lead-based paint is another topic, since the Bureau Health Officer enforces hazard rules for residential structures.

Decide early whether to repair or sell as-is. Repairs mean permits, licensed trades and several weeks, and a failed inspection can cost more time. An as-is sale to a buyer who plans the work puts that burden on the buyer, at a price that reflects it. Either way, tell the buyer what you know.

A buyer of a Harrisburg rental or condemned house takes on city deadlines from the day of recording. A non-condemned rental must be registered within 10 days of purchase, and a condemned property needs permits to lift the condemnation within 30 days of purchase.

The program under Ordinance 1-2017 also requires an inspection at least once every five years, taxes and utilities to be current before a unit can be rented, and a local managing agent when the owner lives more than 50 miles away. The annual landlord license is separate and runs through the Bureau of Licensing, Taxation and Central Support at 717-255-6513.

If you sell a tenant-occupied house, tell the buyer which of these items are paid up.

In Dauphin County the Recorder of Deeds takes the deed and collects the transfer tax. The commonwealth charges 1 percent of the property's value, and a local share goes to school districts and municipalities. The Department of Revenue holds grantor and grantee jointly liable, so have your title company show the split on the closing statement.

Heirs who receive a house through a will, or with none, owe no transfer tax on that inheritance. Their own later sale is a fresh transfer. The current Dauphin County valuation factor from the revenue department is 2.61. A deed for token consideration between tax-exempt parties carries no transfer tax, and checks go to the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.

1. Confirm the parcel is inside the city by checking your tax bill or the county parcel record.
  2. Call the Bureau of Codes at 717-255-6553 and ask what is open on the property, including permits, complaints and any condemnation.
  3. If the house is a rental, gather the lease, deposit details and proof of registration and rental fees.
  4. Ask your title company to show the transfer tax split on the closing statement.
  5. Collect the deed and, for an inherited house, the papers that show who can sign.

Doing this work first gives a buyer clear answers, and clear answers shorten the time between an accepted offer and settlement. A cash buyer does not wait on a lender, so open code or permit items usually set the earliest closing date.

Harrisburg sellers generally pick from three paths.

  • A listing suits a house in decent shape and an owner who can wait for a buyer with loan approval.
  • Going without an agent trims the listing fee, though showings, forms and bargaining fall to you.
  • A cash offer fits a vacant, damaged, inherited or rented property, with the closing date up to you.

Weigh what you would keep after repairs, carrying costs and fees on each path, not the offer alone.

sections.h2: Selling a tenant-occupied or inherited house
sections.html:
With tenants in place, the buyer steps into the lease. Hand over the lease, deposit details and proof that rental fees are paid, and tell the buyer whether the unit is registered. A buyer who keeps renting must register it with the Bureau of Codes within 10 days.

If the house came to you from a relative, start by confirming who has authority to sign for the estate. The inheritance itself triggers no transfer tax, but your sale to a buyer does. Bring the paperwork to the title company early, along with the deed and any open permit records, so the settlement can stay on its date.

faqs.q: Can a Harrisburg house be sold with tenants in place?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer steps into the lease, and one who keeps renting must register the unit with the Bureau of Codes within 10 days of purchase. Hand over your lease, deposit details and proof that rental fees are paid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a condemned Harrisburg house?
faqs.a: Yes. The new owner must secure permits to lift the condemnation within 30 days of purchase, so buyers who can handle repairs are the usual fit.

faqs.q: Is transfer tax due when I inherit a Harrisburg house?
faqs.a: No. Inheritance transfers, with or without a will, are exempt. Your later sale to a buyer carries the 1 percent state tax plus the local share.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about permits on a Harrisburg house?
faqs.a: The Bureau of Codes, at 717-255-6553, handles permits and inspections. Roofing, windows, decks, sheds and any job above $1,000 need one.

faqs.q: Is my Harrisburg mailing address inside the city?
faqs.a: Not always. Lower Paxton, Middle Paxton and other nearby townships carry a Harrisburg mailing name but are separate municipalities with their own codes. Your tax bill or the county parcel record shows which municipality bills you.
